transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-19
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Evan Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Luca Romano (Redwood CSM), Simon LaRue (Artemis, VP Eng), Mina Cho (Head of Platform), Jordan Reyes (SRE)

Summary:
- Purpose: Walk through the recent multi-region stability regression, agree immediate mitigations (safety nets / escrow behaviors), and define operational next steps to prevent long-tail degradations.
- Focus areas: telemetry gaps, autoscale/circuit-breaker policies, KV cache eviction anomalies, and an SLA "insurance" design (safety nets + escrow routing).
- Outcome: Agreement to run a 48-hour canary, Redwood to provide sanitized logs and recommended configs, and a follow-up telemetry deep-dive.

Topics: telemetry gaps; fallback routing; canary/soak test; KV cache corruption theory; autoscaler shock; SLA insurance pattern; audit/KMS concerns.

Action items (reviewed in call): see metadata action_items above.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Evan Morales: All right, thanks everyone for joining. Uh, we'll aim for about 45 minutes. Main goals: recap the incident briefly, then focus on practical safety nets you can enable without major infra changes. Simon, do you want to kick off with your read from Artemis side?
[00:01:12] Simon LaRue: Sure, yeah. Thanks. So, um, last Thursday at 01:10 UTC we saw a spike in 5xxs across our Redwood routes, it lasted roughly 27 minutes, but the real pain point was the long tail — sporadic token timeouts and a bunch of duplicate requests from our edge retriers which amplified load. We saw latency tail go from 180ms to 1.2s for priority routes. We rolled a fallback to smaller model which helped but then some requests still hit KV cache misses and that exacerbated token regen.
[00:02:03] Mina Cho: And to add, our infra team noticed increased memory churn on the cache nodes; sometimes the eviction rate spiked concurrent with the autoscaler kicking in which looked like a cascading effect. Also, we do rotate keys daily with KMS and there was a brief rekey window — not sure if related.
[00:02:37] Priya Nair: Thanks, that's helpful. A couple of quick clarifying q's — when you say duplicate requests from retriers, is that client-side retriers from your SDK, or in-layer retries configured at the gateway?
[00:02:50] Jordan Reyes: It's mostly client SDK. We have a conservative retrier in our mobile client, which escalates on perceived timeouts. The problem was the system went from slow to slow-er, so retries amplified.
[00:03:12] Evan Morales: Got it. The amplification loop is classic. We'll trace amplification separately but today I want to focus on safety nets: circuit breakers at the gateway, request hedging knobs, and a short-lived "escrow" routing where heavy routes get pinned to an isolated pool while we resolve the root cause.
[00:04:05] Simon LaRue: What do you mean by escrow routing? Can Redwood do that without a full Dedicated handoff?
[00:04:18] Priya Nair: Yes — operationally we can create a temporary reserved pool for specific models/routes inside your account (hosted side) and pin traffic there. Think of it as a soft-isolation: it doesn't require on-prem hardware but gives you an isolated runtime with independent autoscaling so noisy neighbors and global autoscaler oscillation don't impact the rest of your traffic.
[00:04:48] Mina Cho: Sounds useful. Any cost bump we should expect for an escrow pool?
[00:04:55] Priya Nair: There's incremental cost, yes, but it's intended to be used as a short-term mitigation. For the canary, you can also run a 10% traffic pin to the pool to validate.
[00:05:20] Jordan Reyes: From SRE side, we prefer config-first mitigations — circuit breakers, lower concurrency, trimming token max-len, and adding a DLQ (dead-letter queue) for malformed or retry-prone requests.
[00:05:39] Luca Romano: Also, we recommended enabling request-level telemetry that surfaces prefix cache hit/miss and KV cache TTL expiration per request in traces — that will make the next RCAs much shorter.
[00:06:05] Simon LaRue: We do have tracing, but we found a telemetry gap: cache TTL expirations weren't surfaced as structured events, they were only in host logs which are aggregated separately.
[00:06:27] Priya Nair: We'll add a hook to emit cache eviction events to your tracing backend, plus an annotation on traces when a request hit the fallback model path. That should be part of the action items.
[00:06:49] Evan Morales: Quick note: there may be a small mismatch between terms — KV cache vs prefix cache — sometimes the logs show "cache miss" but it's actually a tokenization mismatch. The transcriber sometimes swaps terms; sorry — just flagging.
[00:07:10] Mina Cho: No worries. Can we talk about the autoscaler? The pattern looked like scale-up -> immediate throttle -> scale down -> flapping. How do you avoid autoscaler-induced churn?
[00:07:22] Priya Nair: Two mitigations: 1) add a stabilization window and slower cooldown on the autoscaler to avoid flip-flopping, and 2) floor capacity for critical models so you never go below a minimum instance count during high-risk windows. In hosted context we can set an override per model or route.
[00:07:48] Jordan Reyes: Okay, floored capacity makes sense. How do we reconcile that with cost targets?
[00:07:55] Priya Nair: Keep floors only for critical SLAs and use the escrow pool for short-term incidents. Also, enable continuous batching with a smaller per-instance concurrency to keep per-token econ reasonable.
[00:08:15] Simon LaRue: You mentioned circuit breakers and request hedging earlier. For hedging, do you mean sending speculative parallel requests? That could double cost if misconfigured.
[00:08:27] Evan Morales: Good point. Hedge only on critical requests and use a micro-hedge: fire a second request after a small latency threshold only for high-value calls. Use strict cancellation to avoid both completing.
[00:08:42] Mina Cho: Let's go step-by-step. What immediate toggles can we flip this week?
[00:08:50] Priya Nair: Immediate: lower client retrier defaults, enable gateway circuit breaker at 5xx rate threshold of 3% sustained over 60s, and enable a 10% canary to an escrow pool for the top 3 models. Medium: add eviction telemetry and DLQ. Longer: review KMS rotation alignment with runtime startup windows.
[00:09:18] Simon LaRue: About KMS rotation — we rotate keys at 02:00 local time and saw a bump in errors during rotation. Could this cause brief auth failures leading to retries?
[00:09:29] Priya Nair: Potentially. Our client uses cached tokens and if rotation isn't atomic across VMs you can see auth errors. We'll check if the 5xxs correlated to any failed KMS calls in our logs.
[00:09:45] Jordan Reyes: Also, worth noting: we had some older SDK versions on a subset of clients that re-tried more aggressively. We're pushing an SDK update but need a mitigation in meantime.
[00:09:58] Luca Romano: For that, apply a gateway-side throttling rule for SDK-identifiers older than x.y to limit retrier amplification.
[00:10:12] Simon LaRue: Good. Let's talk about postmortem content we want from Redwood. We're expecting a sanitized timeline, root-cause hypotheses, and the set of logs/traces that support those hypotheses.
[00:10:24] Evan Morales: We'll provide a sanitized timeline including per-region latencies, error rates, and cache eviction traces. We will also include sample trace spans that show fallback model invocation. Note that some proper nouns may be fuzzy in the transcript — we'll correct names in docs.
[00:10:41] Mina Cho: On the security side, any concerns about sending logs that reference customer PII? We need redaction.
[00:10:49] Evan Morales: Absolutely. Redwood will sanitize all PII and token values before sharing. We'll use token hashing and replace email/user ids with stable surrogate keys.
[00:11:00] Jordan Reyes: For the 48-hour canary, what metrics should we watch? Latency P95/P99, error budget burn, cache hit ratio, and autoscaler events?
[00:11:12] Priya Nair: Yes: P50/P95/P99 latency, error rate, cache hit ratio, CPU/GPU utilization, instance spin-up rate, and retrier-triggered duplicate requests. We'll also add a synthetic probe for the prefix-cache path to detect tokenization mismatches.
[00:11:32] Simon LaRue: What's the suggested rollback plan if the escrow pool shows regression?
[00:11:38] Priya Nair: If the escrow pool regresses, we can use an automatic fallback to a known-good model version pinned in a lower-capacity but high-stability profile; Redwood supports automatic fallback chains. We'll document the A/B rollback steps and help you run drills.
[00:11:55] Mina Cho: Do you have any recommended canary sizes? 5% vs 10%?
[00:12:00] Evan Morales: Start with 5% for read-only paths, 10% for production if you need better signal. For high-value routes I'd say 10% with short TTL.
[00:12:12] Jordan Reyes: About telemetry gaps: what's the lift to get eviction TTL events into our tracing?
[00:12:18] Priya Nair: Minimal on our side — a config flip to emit structured eviction markers. On your side, if you already ingest traces we can push events in the same format. We'll provide a short script to map events to your backend.
[00:12:35] Simon LaRue: Are there any security/compliance implications for the escrow pool? We still need SOC2 evidence, audit logs, and KMS controls.
[00:12:44] Priya Nair: Escrow pools inherit the same control plane. We can ensure audit logs are exported and KMS/HSM keys are used; we'll include a short SOC2 checklist for the temporary pool.
[00:12:59] Jordan Reyes: I want to call out one more operational pattern: long-tail failures often correlate with large request fan-out from orchestration layers. We should instrument orchestration to tag request origin so we can rate-limit or decouple heavy offline jobs.
[00:13:14] Luca Romano: Agreed. Tagging origins and priority lanes will help us route bulk tasks to lower-cost, sacrificial queues.
[00:13:26] Simon LaRue: OK let's put a priority on the following: 1) get injection of eviction telemetry, 2) enable gateway circuit breakers, 3) set an escrow pool for top models, 4) run the canary and share results.
[00:13:40] Evan Morales: Summarizing next steps: Redwood will send the sanitized timeline and suggested config diffs by 2026-07-22; Priya will attach a recommended autoscaler/circuit-breaker profile and example Terraform snippets; Jordan will run an internal soak and feed back by 2026-07-30. We'll reconvene the week of 2026-07-27 for the telemetry deep-dive.
[00:14:10] Mina Cho: One last question — any quick wins to reduce cost while increasing safety?
[00:14:15] Priya Nair: Yes: use smaller quantized model variants for non-critical routes, enable prefix-KV caching aggressively for stable prompts, and use a short-lived escrow for incidents rather than maintaining dedicated capacity 24/7.
[00:14:33] Simon LaRue: Great. Thanks all.
[00:14:36] Evan Morales: Thanks. We'll send notes + tickets after the call.
[00:14:40] Luca Romano: Thanks everyone.

(Transcription notes: occasional word swaps, e.g., "escrow" used in the call as shorthand for "temporary isolated pool"; some technical terms like KV/cache may be transcribed inconsistently. There were a few instances of crosstalk captured as truncated sentences.)

Recap and deliverables (verbatim for calendar):
- Redwood: sanitized incident timeline + logs, eviction telemetry hook, draft circuit-breaker and autoscaler settings, Terraform snippet for escrow pool (due 2026-07-22).
- Artemis: run 48-hour 10% canary to escrow pool, share soak results (due 2026-07-30).
- Joint: telemetry deep-dive week of 2026-07-27.

End of transcript.
